canonical_statement: The meta-analysis aimed to quantify the efficacy and safety of subcutaneous heparin versus continuous intravenous heparin for initial treatment of deep vein thrombosis.
Eight clinical trials comparing subcutaneous with continuous intravenous heparin in patients with venographically confirmed deep vein thrombosis were identified for the systematic overview.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that twice-daily subcutaneous heparin was more effective and at least as safe as continuous intravenous heparin for initial treatment of deep vein thrombosis and could simplify treatment.

The literature search covered MEDLINE from 1966 through 1991, Current Contents through April 1991, the Science Citation Index from 1989 to February 1991, cited references, and proceedings/abstract books; full manuscripts were sought when only abstracts were available.
Eligible studies directly compared subcutaneous heparin injection with continuous intravenous heparin infusion and required objective confirmation of venous thromboembolism at study entry.

canonical_statement: Methodologic strength was judged against six a priori standards addressing randomized allocation, adequate description of patient groups, adequate treatment description, blinded objective outcome assessment, outcome assessment of all patients, and adequate description of dropouts.
Three investigators independently reviewed and rated each study against the methodologic standards, resolving discrepancies by discussion and consensus.
Studies satisfying five or six quality standards were classified as strong, those satisfying four as moderately strong, and those satisfying fewer than four as weak.
The primary meta-analysis was prespecified to include methodologically strong studies, with a separate analysis adding moderately strong studies.
Study-specific relative risks with 95% confidence intervals were combined using Mantel-Haenszel methods; logistic regression was also used to estimate common odds ratios and test homogeneity.

Across the eight studies, efficacy assessment methods varied: repeat venography predominated, while other studies used combinations of plethysmography/thermography/venography, perfusion lung scanning, or objectively confirmed clinical recurrence.
Approximate average daily heparin doses across the included studies ranged from 24,000 to 37,000 IU per day.

population.label: eight studies in the systematic overview

quantitative_result.effect_measure: range of approximate average daily heparin dose

canonical_statement: Daily heparin doses were similar between routes in three studies, higher in the subcutaneous group in four studies by about 2,100-5,000 IU/day, and higher in the intravenous group in one study.

Within each study, coagulation tests and dose-adjustment criteria were identical for the two treatment groups; heparin treatment lasted 5-14 days, and oral anticoagulant therapy was typically started 3 days after heparin initiation.
Seven of the eight included investigations used randomization.

population.label: eight studies in the systematic overview

canonical_statement: Six studies were rated methodologically strong and two moderately strong; none were rated weak.

canonical_statement: The homogeneity test was statistically significant for efficacy (P < 0.001), indicating substantial between-study inconsistency in efficacy effects.
The homogeneity test was not statistically significant for safety (P > 0.6).
The authors acknowledged that the confidence interval around the pooled efficacy risk reduction was relatively broad.
The pooled efficacy analysis combined different clinical and subclinical outcome measures under a common definition of thromboembolic progression.

The mean incidence of major hemorrhage across the pooled studies was 4.1% in subcutaneous-heparin groups and 5.2% in intravenous-heparin groups, but the overall safety relative risk was imprecise and not statistically significant.

The meta-analysis reports that, in the Hull trial, recurrent venous thromboembolism risk was about 15-fold higher when APTT remained below 1.5 times control for at least 24 hours from therapy initiation than when APTT response was adequate.

population.label: patients in the Hull et al. trial with subtherapeutic versus adequate APTT response

canonical_statement: Comparable APTT-response subgroup analyses could not be performed across the other studies because APTT was measured infrequently or by differing methods.
A subgroup analysis by heparin salt showed no trend favoring calcium or sodium heparin; the underlying data were not shown.

Efficacy effects were heterogeneous across studies; the authors identified the Hull trial as the apparent source of the inconsistency and attributed its divergent result to early subtherapeutic heparin levels in the subcutaneous group.

After screening multiple bibliographic and meeting sources and contacting investigators, the authors reported finding no additional eligible studies and stated that they believed publication bias had not occurred.
The authors concluded that subcutaneous heparin was more efficacious and at least as safe as intravenous heparin for initial treatment of deep vein thrombosis.
The authors proposed that broader use of subcutaneous heparin could simplify treatment and support research into self-administration in outpatient or home settings.
